A retirement income replacement ratio needs a cash budget: distinguish gross pay, net receipts and spending

Reconcile an original working-year budget with retirement spending, then compare a chosen gross-income ratio after an explicit tax assumption and test continuing debt and new costs.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 6 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Reconcile a current annual cash budget with one retirement-year spending scenario

Interactive planning lab

Retirement spending cash need$50,000
Gross retirement receipts implied by the chosen tax fraction$62,500
Implied gross receipts as a share of current gross pay62.50%
Chosen gross ratio: cash excess (+) or gap (−)$6,000

Original hypothetical annual cash-budget reconciliation, with all amounts in one common price basis. It is a comparison of one working-year budget with one retirement-year budget, not a multi-year projection. Current deductions, take-home saving, ending work costs, ending debt payments and continuing cash needs are disjoint uses of gross pay. All four percentage inputs use current gross pay as their denominator. Current deductions exclude the saving entered separately. The residual continuing budget includes any debt service or work-related cost that will continue. The stated ending costs actually cease in this scenario, and the current saving transfer stops. Additional retirement spending is added to the continuing budget. Modeled retirement receipts are one assumed gross taxable cash stream with the same flat average tax fraction at every tested income. The tax fraction is an entered assumption, not a marginal tax bracket, a withholding rate or a calculation under current law. No pension entitlement, benefit reduction, payroll contribution rule, account-specific tax treatment, tax-free withdrawal, return of capital, spouse’s income, capital balance or withdrawal strategy is calculated. The gross ratio comparison first subtracts its assumed retirement tax, then compares net cash with spending. A positive difference is cash excess in this one-year budget, not proof that retirement is funded. Inflation between dates, longevity, changing spending phases, investment uncertainty, ongoing saving and large one-time costs require separate schedules. The input bounds keep the current continuing budget positive; the derived retirement gross ratio may exceed 100% and is not capped.

The central idea

A percentage of former gross pay does not specify the cash needed for retirement bills. Identify which current payments end, which continue and how gross receipts become spendable cash.

01

Write down the numerator and denominator before using a replacement percentage

A retirement income replacement ratio often compares an annual retirement income amount with an earlier annual employment income amount. The percentage is incomplete unless both amounts have clear definitions.

Are they gross amounts before income tax, or cash available after tax? Does the employment reference include one person or a household? Is the retirement amount an income target, a spending estimate or a withdrawal from savings? The same percentage can describe different questions.

This article chooses one explicit comparison: gross retirement receipts divided by current gross annual employment pay. The default 70% setting is an assumption to test, rather than a personal recommendation or a claim about the typical retiree.

All figures use one common price basis. They compare the structure of one working-year budget with one retirement-year budget. They do not automatically project a current salary into the future, allow for inflation between dates or determine how many years the plan must last.

02

Find the current cash commitments hidden inside gross pay

The invented working budget begins with CAD 100,000 of gross annual pay. Tax and other pay deductions use CAD 25,000. Saving transferred from take-home cash uses another CAD 15,000.

The scenario separately identifies CAD 5,000 of work-related costs and CAD 10,000 of debt payments that are assumed to end before retirement. After those four disjoint uses, CAD 45,000 remains for continuing annual cash needs.

The first waterfall shows the entire reconciliation: CAD 100,000 − CAD 25,000 − CAD 15,000 − CAD 5,000 − CAD 10,000 = CAD 45,000. No category can appear in two steps.

Every percentage control in this working budget uses gross pay as its denominator. The 15% saving input therefore means CAD 15,000 from take-home cash, rather than 15% of the remaining CAD 75,000. Saving already included in another deduction must not be entered again.

03

Replace a broad ratio with the spending that actually continues

The continuing CAD 45,000 budget does not have to equal retirement spending. The example adds CAD 5,000 of new annual retirement costs, giving a retirement spending cash need of CAD 50,000.

FCAC’s retirement-planning guidance recommends comparing current spending with expected retirement spending. Work costs may change, while activities, travel and other plans can introduce different expenses.

In the model, the additional amount is incremental. If a trip is already represented in the continuing budget, adding its full cost again would overstate the total. Conversely, a new recurring expense should not be omitted merely because it was absent during employment.

This construction can produce retirement spending above the former continuing budget even when gross retirement receipts are below former salary. Here, CAD 50,000 is about 111.1% of the CAD 45,000 continuing cash budget. That comparison has a different denominator from a gross-pay replacement ratio.

04

Translate the spending need into gross receipts using an explicit assumption

The model treats all retirement receipts as one gross taxable cash stream. It assumes an average tax fraction of 20%, leaving 80% available for the stated non-income-tax spending.

To provide CAD 50,000 of spending cash under that assumption, required gross receipts are CAD 50,000 ÷ 0.8 = CAD 62,500. Relative to CAD 100,000 of current gross pay, the implied gross replacement ratio is 62.5%.

The tax funding is CAD 12,500. Adding 20% directly to CAD 50,000 would instead produce CAD 60,000, which leaves only CAD 48,000 after a 20% deduction. The fraction applies to gross receipts, so division by the retained share is required.

This is arithmetic under an entered tax assumption. It is not a calculation of a Canadian tax return, withholding, marginal brackets, credits or benefit reductions. Actual retirement cash can come from sources with different tax treatment, and that mix needs a separate source-by-source calculation.

05

Compare the chosen ratio after tax with the spending budget

The default chosen ratio is 70%. Multiplying current gross pay by 70% gives CAD 70,000 of modeled gross retirement receipts. Applying the assumed 20% tax fraction leaves CAD 56,000.

Compare that net amount with the CAD 50,000 spending need. The one-year difference is CAD 6,000 of cash excess. The signed comparison chart shows the net cash, the spending need and their difference as separate quantities.

That result does not establish that 70% is necessary, sufficient for every year or obtainable from the household’s actual resources. The example has not supplied pension entitlements, investment balances or a sustainable withdrawal schedule.

A lower chosen ratio can produce a negative cash difference. The chart retains that gap rather than setting it to zero. A derived required ratio above 100% is also left visible: substantial new costs or a different tax assumption can imply more gross receipts than the stated working-pay reference.

06

Remove a payment only when it actually ends

The default assumes CAD 10,000 of current annual debt payments has ended before retirement. It removes the whole cash payment, which may include both principal and interest. A future payoff date must support that assumption.

If the debt payment will continue, change the ending-debt share from 10% to zero. The residual continuing budget rises to CAD 55,000, which now includes that ongoing payment. Adding the same CAD 5,000 of new costs gives CAD 60,000 of retirement spending cash need.

At the same 20% tax fraction, the implied gross receipts rise to CAD 75,000. The chosen 70% ratio still supplies only CAD 56,000 of net cash, producing a CAD 4,000 gap instead of the previous excess.

Apply the same discipline to commuting, professional costs, saving transfers and other commitments. A cost can cease, continue or be replaced by another cost. Its category label does not prove which cash schedule will apply to the household.

07

Use the annual reconciliation as a starting point for a dated plan

The matrix varies additional spending and the average tax assumption while retaining the working-budget shares. It demonstrates sensitivity rather than estimating how likely any cell is to occur.

For an actual plan, use the right price year for income and spending, then build the payment calendar. Income sources may begin in different months, a debt may end partway through a year, and one-time purchases can require more accessible cash than an annual average suggests.

Next consider inflation, changing spending phases, longevity and uncertainty in investment resources. The annual gross amount derived here is not a portfolio value, an investment return or a withdrawal-rate recommendation.

Review the budget against current records and the actual tax treatment of each receipt. A clearly defined replacement ratio can summarize a completed calculation, but the spending, deductions and timing should remain inspectable underneath it. That lets the plan respond to a real change in commitments instead of relying on an unchanged headline percentage.

They do not calculate current tax law, pension benefits, a portfolio withdrawal rate or lifetime retirement funding.
